title: Foxes in the city: wild neighbours after dark
description: When the streets empty, red foxes pad out of gardens and railway banks to patrol the city they share with us — same species as the snow fox of the countryside, living a completely different life.

body.heading: The night shift
paragraphs: Urban foxes keep rural hours in reverse: they rest by day in quiet corners — under sheds, in overgrown gardens — and emerge at dusk to hunt and scavenge. A city offers rich pickings: fallen fruit, spilled bins, rodents, and earthworms after rain.

Studies of city foxes show territories far smaller than country ones, because food is packed so densely. A fox family can live its whole life within a few streets without ever meeting the humans above it.

body.heading: Good neighbours, wild animals
paragraphs: The golden rule is to enjoy them at a distance. Feeding foxes by hand teaches them to approach people, which ends badly for the fox; watching quietly from a window teaches you their routes, their cubs in spring, and their alarm bark — a short, sharp triple-yap in the dark.
If you spot a fox at dusk, note the time and place. Foxes are creatures of routine, and the patient watcher is often rewarded with the same animal, same corner, same hour, tomorrow.

takeaway: City foxes live a whole wild life within a few streets of us — watch quietly from a distance, never feed by hand, and their routines will reveal themselves.
